short: Montana has no dedicated AI act, but its 2025 legislature passed the Right to Compute Act, government-AI limits, and deepfake laws, while a 1973 consumer protection law and 2023 genetic privacy act already reach AI conduct.
title: Montana AI Laws
subtitle: What Montana's Right to Compute Act, government-AI limits, deepfake rules, and older privacy laws actually cover
body_html:
Montana has no single, named AI act like Colorado or Utah. Its 2025 legislature instead passed a cluster of narrower AI bills covering government use, elections, deepfakes, and neural data, while a 2023 genetic privacy law and a 1973 consumer protection act already reach a lot of AI conduct on their own. The state leans toward protecting the right to use computing and AI rather than restricting it, but the specific harms lawmakers worried about are now addressed in statute.

What the legislature did

Montana's legislature meets for about 90 days every odd year, and the 2023 session produced no AI-specific bills. A 2023-2024 interim Law and Justice Committee study on AI set up a much busier 2025 session, where lawmakers introduced roughly a dozen AI-related bills and several became law.

Senate Bill 212, the Right to Compute Act from Senator Daniel Zolnikov, was signed April 16, 2025. It declares a fundamental right to privately own and use computing resources and requires any state restriction on that right to survive strict scrutiny. An early version would have forced AI-controlled critical infrastructure to shut down and revert to human control, but that mandate was amended out, leaving a lighter requirement to adopt a risk management policy.

House Bill 178, from Representative Braxton Mitchell, limits state and local agencies from using AI for discriminatory profiling or cognitive manipulation, requires disclosure when AI produces material the public sees, and requires human review before an AI recommendation affects someone's rights, with carve-outs for sensitive law enforcement work. It passed near-unanimously and was signed May 5, 2025.

On elections, Senate Bill 25 requires disclosure of AI-generated content in campaign communications and bars undisclosed deepfakes of candidates within 60 days of an election. Signed May 8, 2025, it is already being tested in federal court, where a PAC treasurer argues the disclosure mandate is compelled speech violating the First Amendment, with a ruling expected after an August 2025 hearing in Helena. Three more May 2025 signings round out the group: Senate Bill 413 criminalizes disclosure of sexually explicit AI-generated media, House Bill 513 extends name, voice, and likeness protections against unauthorized AI replication, and House Bill 514 criminalizes real and fabricated sexually explicit images.

Not everything survived. House Bill 556, which would have regulated AI in health insurance coverage decisions, and Senate Bill 452, which would have required AI-use disclosures from online media manufacturers, were both tabled in committee and died.

What already applies without a dedicated AI act

Montana's Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Act, in place since 1973, prohibits deceptive and unfair business practices regardless of whether AI is involved, and it has already been invoked over AI specifically, discussed below. The Montana Human Rights Act likewise applies to AI-driven discrimination in employment or public accommodations.

Montana's constitutional right of privacy, Article II, Section 10, is broader than most states' and Montana courts have applied it expansively to government and, in some contexts, private data handling. That backdrop matters for AI systems trained on or making decisions from Montanans' personal data, even without an AI-specific statute.

The 2023 Genetic Information Privacy Act, one of the first laws of its kind nationally, requires consent before genetic data is collected or shared. Senate Bill 163 amended it in 2025 to add neurotechnology data from devices that record nervous-system activity such as EEG signals, requiring consent and data localization starting October 1, 2025, though only for entities already covered by the genetic law. Montana's Consumer Data Privacy Act, in effect since 2024 and strengthened by Senate Bill 297, gives consumers the right to opt out of profiling, reaching automated decision-making tools that profile Montana residents.

What the Attorney General has done

In February 2024, Attorney General Austin Knudsen sent Google a formal letter demanding answers about its Gemini AI system, citing the consumer protection act and the Montana Human Rights Act. He argued Gemini's outputs, including refusing some image requests and mischaracterizing historical events, amounted to deceptive marketing given Google's accuracy claims, and posed 15 questions with a response deadline. That letter, not a lawsuit, is the most concrete AI-specific action the Montana Department of Justice has taken.

What this means

Montana does not need a named AI act to have AI law. An organization operating there can already face government-use restrictions, election and deepfake disclosure rules, neural-data consent requirements, or plain old consumer protection and constitutional privacy exposure, depending on what it builds and who it touches. The Right to Compute Act adds a countervailing signal: Montana wants AI restrictions to clear a high bar, not a low one.
